1:
The address is to hills, and the voices explain why. Gill takes them for the hill country of Judah and prefers concerning to against, since these later oracles are in their favour; the country being cleared of men, nothing was left to speak to. Henry makes it sharper: the prophet had once been sent against these same hills, and now that God returns in mercy he must speak comfortably to them, the people being gone and the ground alone left, which the conquerors could not carry away. Clarke calls it a beautiful personification; Ellicott adds that mountains here stand for land and people together, holding the contrast with the mountain named just before.

Who the enemy is divides them. Clarke is specific: the Edomites had seized the high ground and its fortresses during the captivity, to shut the Jews out if they returned. Wesley allows many enemies but says they conspired so far that the prophet treats them as one. Ellicott resists the narrowing. The phrase about ancient high places is near enough the everlasting hills of two old blessings to be an allusion, and the enemy is a general term; the following verses make it the heathen at large, who saw the land desolate, concluded the promise had failed, and reckoned it theirs.

The verbs are worked over. Ellicott corrects swallowed up to pant for, the word taken from the snuffing of wild beasts, and would read empty out rather than cast out, since casting a land out for a prey makes no sense. Keil and Delitzsch render the boast flatly, that the everlasting heights have fallen to them and Israel has come into the talk of the tongue. Henry supplies the scene: the neighbours flew to the spoil as to a shipwreck, nobody thinking it a crime to strip an Israelite, and the boast meant that neither antiquity nor sanctity nor fortification had saved the place.

Against that comes an oath. Ellicott notes that the lifted hand means swearing, and that the reproach the Israelites were made to carry now turns back on those who inflicted it; Wesley calls it swearing in wrath and names the three neighbouring peoples.

Then the hills are told to bear fruit. Ellicott hears both certainty and nearness in it, the land putting out produce because the people are coming; Clarke presses harder, saying the return was so determined that one might be as sure of it as if the families were crossing the border, though fifty-eight of the seventy years were still to run. Gill has the mountains tilled and sown, men multiplied, the beasts restored. On the promise to do better than at the beginning both baulk at a literal reading. Clarke, following another, doubts it can be shown fulfilled between the return and the birth of Christ, the colouring being too high and the whole suiting gospel times better. Ellicott grants a partial fulfilment after the exile and in the Maccabean age, but finds the language outrunning the history, so the earthly blessings become shadow and type.

The last reproach is that the land eats its own people. Ellicott traces it to the old spies' report, in the prophet's mind though put to another use, and explains its currency: Israel had suffered so often that the heathen, missing the real cause, blamed the soil. Wesley answers with the blessing that the country will raise sons and daughters and the reproach cease. Ellicott closes with two observations. The first is a play on words English cannot carry, two verbs alike in their letters but for a transposition, one meaning to bereave, the other to cause to fall. The second is that the whole prophecy assumes an Edom still standing and gloating, so it cannot be waiting on a literal future fulfilment, that nation having long since disappeared and no later people being able to stand in its place.
16:
A fresh oracle begins, and Keil and Delitzsch lay out its whole argument before commenting on any part. Israel defiled its land and was scattered for it; but because the scattering profaned God's name among the nations, he will act for that name's sake — gathering them, cleansing them, sanctifying them by the gift of his Spirit, then blessing them until both the nations and Israel know who he is. They treat the opening formula as marking an independent word, bound to what precedes as the motive of the restoration, and locate its kernel in the promise of clean water and a new heart.

The defilement grounds everything. Gill describes what was lost, a land of plenty also chosen for God's worship; Henry says God's eye was on it, and presses the phrase their own way as meaning the way of their own choosing, so that the blame is theirs. Clarke states the counterfactual: had they stayed faithful they would never have been removed, but they polluted the land and God gave up land and people to the destroyers. Ellicott supplies the principle, that the land is consecrated ground which the people's sin defiles, and identifies the comparison as a woman set apart for uncleanness and kept from the sanctuary until her purifying. Wesley reads it as exclusion from the congregation for some great sin.

Then the exile itself becomes the offence, and the voices differ on how. Clarke has the exiles so fallen that God was blasphemed on their account, the onlookers asking what being could own such a people. Ellicott declines that as the primary reading. They profaned the name, he says, by the bare fact of captivity: the heathen took their God for a national one, saw the nation dispersed and in distress, and concluded he had been unable to protect it — so that vindicating his name required their restoration. Wesley puts the taunt in their mouths: these slaves call themselves the people of the Lord and claim a land they were driven out of.

The pity that follows is directed at the name. Gill makes it a concern for God's own honour; Wesley says the sins deserved cutting off, but destroying them would have let the heathen draw conclusions against his power and truth.

Ellicott turns the refusal against a modern objection. Since this is the constant burden of the teaching given to Israel throughout their history, it is idle to complain that Scripture makes them heaven's favourites in the manner of other national legends; the narrative is unlike any other, presenting one nation chosen as the means of a purpose reaching the whole world, chastised without pause, the mass repeatedly set aside, a remnant purified for that purpose rather than its own. Henry reaches it from the captives' side: their unworthiness was the discouragement, and the answer is that God acts for his own name; the restoration being a type of redemption, the end of every step of salvation is the glory of God.

Sanctifying the name is then defined. Gill takes it as clearing the name of the charges laid against it, and notes that God chose to vindicate it by grace rather than by the punishment he might justly have inflicted. Clarke locates the demonstration in the people, since changing their hearts and conduct is how God shows his hatred of vice and love of holiness. Wesley says they had given the heathen occasion to think meanly of him, and he will show himself as great as good. Ellicott ends on a textual point with a doctrinal edge: the Hebrew as it stands reads in your eyes where many authorities read in their eyes, and though either yields good sense, the first brings out that God must be sanctified in the eyes of his own people before he can be sanctified through them in anyone else's.
24:
Nobody takes the gathering as merely the return from Babylon. Gill has them fetched out of the nations they were carried to and those they live among still, the work completed at the conversion of the Jews in the latter day, and reads the phrase besides as an image of grace calling a people out of the world. Clarke says it flatly: since the Jews are scattered to this day through heathen, Muslim and Christian countries alike, it is out of these that they are to be gathered and set back in their land.

The clean water divides the tile. Gill argues at length that it is not baptism, as one father held, since baptism is not performed by sprinkling and is administered by men rather than being an operation of God; nor is it the renewing grace of the Spirit, which the next verse covers. He settles on the blood of Christ. Clarke takes the opposite line and makes the water the influences of the Spirit, the filthiness covering every pollution outward and inward and the idols false worship, false opinions and false hopes alike. Ellicott hears a priest speaking, referring to the washings of the law in their symbolic force rather than to any one of them; the primary reference is to cleansing from idolatry, and to the people as a body, though what follows requires it to reach individuals too. That symbolism, he adds, later produced the washing of proselytes, taken up by the forerunner and made the initiatory sacrament. Henry keeps both senses, blood sprinkled on the conscience as the water of purification removed a ceremonial stain, and the grace of the Spirit sprinkled on the whole soul; Wesley quotes him word for word.

On the new heart they converge. Gill treats heart and spirit as one thing renewed, carrying a new principle of life, a new will, and affections that bring new sorrows as well as new delights. Clarke divides the two, giving the heart the affections and the spirit the mind, understanding, judgment and will, and is severe on what is removed: a heart hard, impenetrable and cold, frozen to good and slow to credit God's words, taken away entire, since nobody holds the new heart and the old at once. Wesley describes a frame moulded into compliance with the whole will of God, taking the impress as soft wax takes a seal.

The Spirit that follows makes obedience possible, and the accents differ. Clarke builds a hierarchy in which the Spirit actuates the new spirit and that the new affections, so that passion is ruled by reason and reason by the Spirit; and he presses the result, that the cause is evidenced by the effect, since walking in the statutes means conduct actually regulated by them — the birthright of every believer, not a promise to Israel only. Wesley is careful to leave the will its part: the causing is sweet and powerful yet without compulsion, because a spirit already framed to a disposition suitable to God's holiness readily concurs.

The last promise returns to the ground. Gill has them not merely brought in but settled, and values the land as a gift promised to the fathers, so that its restoration proves the promise was not forgotten. Ellicott explains why an earthly promise is still needed here: the people could not yet seek spiritual good except as attached to temporal good, the temporal being in providence the necessary means to the spiritual, so the restoration had to be promised and in due time literally given. Clarke reads the covenant formula as an exchange, a people wholly given up and a God who fills them. Wesley marks the order and will not have it reversed, that then and not before are these promises to be fulfilled; the closing words he calls the foundation of the top-stone of a believer's happiness.
29:
A further cleansing is promised after the heart has been changed, and Ellicott asks why, since they have been washed and given a new heart already. It cannot be the idolatry purged away, he answers, and becomes plain if taken for the ordinary sinfulness of a man, continually renewed and so needing continual forgiveness. Wesley reads the tense the same way, that God will continue to save, packing into it justification, entire sanctification, and fitness for glory. Gill distinguishes deliverance from the dominion of sin by grace and from its guilt by the blood, and reads the plenty that follows on two levels, orchard and field literally, and the increase of gifts in the churches spiritually.

Clarke puts to himself the objection the passage invites: will people saved so far not grow proud, and not undervalue the blood once they no longer need it? The verse about self-loathing is his answer. Such people never forget the pit they came out of, so pride is impossible; they never forgive themselves for sinning against so good a God, and the blood is more precious than ever, since it takes the same power to sustain a creation as to make one, and the same Christ to keep clean who cleansed. Gill catalogues what will be remembered, the breaches of the law before the exile and the self-made righteousness after, and observes that the goodness of God refreshes the memory, so that sins never counted sins return with all their weight. On the refusal to act for their sakes he is blunt: no merit, only grace.

The land is rebuilt, and the voices climb from soil to symbol. Gill has the waste ground made fruitful again, and offers the spiritual reading beside it, the fallow ground of the heart ploughed and sown. Clarke compresses the movement into a sentence: a land desolate by sin becomes like the garden of Eden by righteousness, the blast removed and the blessing come. Ellicott weighs the comparison. It may mean no more than that the land became prosperous; but taken with what precedes it seems to look forward to a condition in which man is once more wholly free of sin, the state the church has prepared for in every age.

Then a condition is attached, and that there is one surprises them. Gill states the principle: God has promised and will perform, yet expects his people to apply to him and plead the promise. He also records a reading of the versions that reverses the direction, making God the one who seeks out Israel. Clarke turns the verse into an answer to who shall have such blessings: they who pray, seek earnestly, and strive to enter by the narrow gate. Ellicott finds the point in the contrast with earlier chapters, where God refused to be inquired of by a people whose heart was far from him, and now, having given a new heart, hears. Wesley says only that a repeated promise does not excuse anyone from asking.

The chapter closes on flocks. Gill takes the figure from animals consecrated for sacrifice and driven up to the city at the annual feasts, especially the passover, when every household needed a lamb, and cites the tens of thousands one king gave at a single feast. Ellicott agrees the point is a vivid idea of numbers, but notes an added fitness, those flocks being devoted to the Lord. Wesley presses further: increase of population is honourable only where the people are dedicated as a holy flock, crowds being a lovely sight in God's temple. Clarke takes it for the church without spot and the city from above, and ends with a declaration he refuses to apologise for: he has read the chapter throughout of the redemption under the new covenant and not of the return from Babylon, no period of the nation's history since answering to it.
